messages.content:
1. **References in the document are either specific or non-specific.**  
   → This is stated in section “4 Overview” where the text explains that references are categorized as specific (with publication date/edition/version, etc.) or non-specific.

2. **For a specific reference, subsequent revisions do not apply.**  
   → The passage says that if a reference is specific, later updates are not used.

3. **For a non-specific reference, the latest version applies.**  
   → The passage specifies the rule for non-specific references: use the newest version.

4. **For non-specific references to 3GPP documents, “latest version” is restricted to the same Release as the present document.**  
   → The passage adds an interpretation rule for 3GPP (including GSM) documents: latest version must be within the same Release.

5. **ETSI ES 282 001 (V3.4.1) is referenced as “NGN Functional Architecture Release 1” (TISPAN).**  
   → Appears in the numbered reference list as [1] with that title.

6. **ETSI ES 282 007 (V2.1.1) is referenced as “IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS); Functional architecture” (TISPAN).**  
   → Appears as [2] in the reference list.

7. **ETSI TS 182 012 (V2.1.4) is referenced as “IMS-based PSTN/ISDN Emulation Subsystem; Functional architecture” (TISPAN).**  
   → Appears as [3] in the reference list.

8. **ETSI ETS 300 738 (First edition) is referenced as a Human Factors (HF) MMI standard for public network supplementary services.**  
   → Appears as [4] in the reference list.

9. **3GPP TS 23.228 is referenced and concerns IMS stage 2.**  
   → Appears as [5] with the title “IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS); Stage 2”.

10. **3GPP TS 23.167 is referenced and concerns IMS emergency sessions.**  
   → Appears as [6] with that title.

11. **3GPP TS 33.203 is referenced and concerns 3G security access security for IP-based services.**  
   → Appears as [7] with the title “3G Security; Access security for IP-based services”.

12. **IETF RFC 3323 (December 2002) is referenced for SIP privacy mechanisms.**  
   → Appears as [9] in the reference list.

13. **IETF RFC 3325 (December 2002) is referenced for SIP private extensions for asserted identity in trusted networks.**  
   → Appears as [10] in the reference list.

14. **IETF RFC 5031 (January 2008) is referenced for a URN for emergency and other well-known services.**  
   → Appears as [19] in the reference list.

15. **IETF RFC 3966 (December 2004) is referenced for the “tel” URI for telephone numbers.**  
   → Appears as [21] in the reference list.

16. **IETF RFC 3261 (July 2002) is referenced as the “SIP: Session Initiation Protocol” specification.**  
   → Appears as [22] in the reference list.

17. **IETF RFC 4967 (July 2007) is referenced for the Dial String parameter for SIP URIs.**  
   → Appears as [23] in the reference list.

18. **IETF RFC 7316 (July 2014) is referenced for SIP P-Private-Network-Indication header (P-Header).**  
   → Appears as [24] in the reference list.

19. **The document uses definitions from 3GPP TS 22.519 [14], 3GPP TS 24.229 [15], and ETSI TS 183 043 [16].**  
   → This is stated in section “3.1 Definitions.”

20. **The document’s abbreviations are the ones listed in section 3.2.**  
   → This is stated in section “3.2 Abbreviations” (“the following abbreviations apply”).

21. **Hosted Enterprise Services (HES) is a solution where an NGN hosts all business communication capabilities.**  
   → The “4 Overview” section begins by defining HES in exactly these terms.

22. **HES connects those capabilities to endpoints connected to multiple access points.**  
   → The HES definition continues by describing endpoints and their access points.

23. **HES is also known as IP Centrex.**  
   → The passage explicitly says this type of solution is also called IP Centrex.

24. **In the simplest configuration, all endpoints connect to a TISPAN NGN IP-CAN.**  
   → The next paragraph under “4 Overview” describes the simplest setup.

25. **In the simplest configuration, endpoints may be SIP phones.**  
   → The same paragraph lists SIP phones as one possible endpoint type.

26. **In the simplest configuration, endpoints may be legacy phones (Analogue or ISDN).**  
   → The paragraph also lists legacy phones (Analogue/ISDN).

27. **In the simplest configuration, legacy phones connect through a gateway.**  
   → The text says legacy phones are “connected to a gateway.”

28. **In the simplest configuration, HES services are provided by application servers.**  
   → The text states “All services by HES are provided by application servers…”

29. **In the simplest configuration, those application servers use standard IMS procedures.**  
   → The passage specifies the method for providing services: “using standard IMS procedures.”

30. **Users may access services specific to their enterprise.**  
   → The text says users can access enterprise-specific services.

31. **Users may also access services available to any other IMS users.**  
   → The text adds that HES users can access services open to other IMS users.

32. **In more complex configurations, some endpoints may connect to a 3GPP IPCAN.**  
   → The “In more complex configurations…” paragraph lists 3GPP IPCAN as one option.

33. **In more complex configurations, some endpoints may connect to a circuit-switched network.**  
   → The same paragraph also lists circuit-switched network connectivity.

34. **The circuit-switched network connects to IMS via an MGCF.**  
   → The paragraph explains the link: circuit-switched network → IMS via MGCF.

35. **Endpoints on heterogeneous access networks may be served by the same HES.**  
   → The text states this as a property of complex configurations.

36. **Endpoints served by a HES must be able to set up a session.**  
   → The passage uses “shall have the ability to setup a session.”

37. **Session setup requires identifying the communication target.**  
   → The text says session setup identifies the communication target.

38. **One way to identify the target is via a SIP URI of the form “user @domain”.**  
   → This is listed as the first bullet under target identification.

39. **Another way is via an E.164 telephone number.**  
   → This is listed as a second bullet option.

40. **Another way is via a number within a private numbering plan.**  
   → This is listed as a third bullet option.

41. **Another way is via local service numbers.**  
   → This is listed as a fourth bullet option.

42. **SIP stands for “Session Initiation Protocol.”**  
   → In the abbreviations table, SIP is defined with that expansion.

43. **IMS stands for “IP Multimedia Subsystem.”**  
   → In the abbreviations table, IMS is defined with that expansion.

44. **NGN stands for “Next Generation Network.”**  
   → In the abbreviations table, NGN is defined as Next Generation Network.

45. **UE stands for “User Equipment.”**  
   → In the abbreviations table, UE is defined as User Equipment.

46. **PSTN stands for “Public Switched Telephony Network.”**  
   → In the abbreviations table, PSTN is defined as Public Switched Telephony Network.

Which two categories of references are explicitly mentioned in the document’s overview?
The two categories explicitly mentioned are specific references and non-specific references.
